column2: A rain gauge fills each week. Who could use its readings to plan a school garden?
column3: The person deciding when to water
column6: Rain measurements help gardeners decide whether extra water is needed.

column2: A shoemaker tests soles on a smooth floor. What useful feature is being checked?
column3: How well the soles grip
column5: How bright the shoe box is
column6: Testing grip helps a shoemaker choose soles that reduce slipping.

column2: A beach closes after water tests find pollution. What guided this decision?
column3: Evidence from the water tests
column4: The colour of the beach sign
column6: Test results can guide decisions that protect people.

column2: A school bell is hard to hear in the far classroom. What could staff investigate?
column3: Where the bell can be heard clearly
column5: How many windows are painted blue
column6: Checking sound in different places can help improve a warning system.

column2: A worker tests handles before choosing one for a hot pan. What would be useful to find out?
column3: Which handle stays cooler
column4: Which handle has the longest name
column6: Testing materials helps people choose a handle that is safer to hold.

column2: A gardener sees frost on the same exposed bed on several cold mornings. What might help protect new plants there?
column3: Covering them before another frosty night
column5: Moving them there after frost appears
column6: A repeated frost pattern helps the gardener plan protection in advance.

column2: A lifeguard checks tide information before a beach activity. What can this help predict?
column3: How the water level may change
column6: Tide records show repeating changes in water level.

column2: An optician tests a child's sight before choosing glasses. Why test first?
column3: To find out what help the child needs
column5: To make every child use the same lenses
column6: Observations from a sight test guide the choice of lenses.

column2: Water beads on a waxy leaf but spreads on paper. What could you ask next?
column3: Does water spread the same way on both surfaces?
column4: Which surface has the nicest name?
column6: The question follows a visible difference and can be checked with drops of water.

column2: A sponge springs back after a gentle squeeze. Predict what a second gentle squeeze may do.
column3: It may spring back again
column6: The first squeeze provides a reason to expect the sponge to return to its shape.

column2: A seed pod rattles when shaken. What question could help explain the sound?
column3: Does the sound change when the seeds cannot move?
column4: Is the pod the best one?
column5: Does the pod enjoy being shaken?
column6: Comparing moving and held-still seeds can help explore what makes the sound.

column2: A paper strip bends under one block. A folded strip stays up. What could you predict about another folded strip?
column3: It may hold one block without bending much
column4: It must hold every block in the room
column6: The first comparison supports a cautious prediction about another folded strip.

column2: Snails were seen under damp leaves on three mornings. What question follows this pattern?
column3: Are more snails found under damp leaves than dry leaves?
column4: Which snail has the best shell?
column5: Do snails know the days of the week?
column6: The class can compare counts while leaving snails undisturbed.

column2: A wind spinner turns quickly in a breeze. What might happen when the breeze stops?
column3: The spinner may slow down
column4: The spinner will turn into paper
column6: The observation links moving air with the spinner turning.

column2: A wet footprint fades from the path. Which question could a class explore?
column3: How long does the footprint stay visible?
column5: Does the footprint like the path?
column6: The time until the mark fades can be observed and recorded.

column2: A foil boat holds blocks, then sinks when another is added. What could you investigate next?
column3: Would a wider foil boat hold more blocks?
column6: Changing boat width gives a new question about the observed result.

column2: A class will observe worms in soil. How should the worms be treated?
column3: Handle them gently as instructed and return them safely
column5: Pull them to see if they stretch
column6: Safe investigations also care for living things.

column2: For a leaf-rubbing activity, where should paper and crayons be placed?
column3: On a clear, steady work surface
column4: On the edge of a full water tub
column6: A clear, steady surface helps prevent spills and trips.

column2: Two children share a timer and a notebook. What plan helps them work together?
column3: Agree who times and who records
column5: Start before anyone knows their job
column6: Agreeing on roles helps the group follow the investigation steps.

column2: A class watches a feather fall. How can they keep the test safe?
column3: Drop it from a reachable height as instructed
column6: A reachable release point avoids a fall risk.

column2: A teacher provides a tray for breaking dry clay. Why use the tray?
column3: To keep small pieces in one place
column4: To make every piece the same size
column5: To turn clay into a liquid
column6: The tray contains pieces and makes clean-up easier.

column2: Children will take turns at a sound station. Which plan protects everyone's hearing?
column3: Use gentle sounds and wait for a turn
column4: Play every instrument beside one ear
column6: Gentle sounds and orderly turns make a safer investigation.

column2: A class compares paper spinners. What should they decide before dropping them?
column3: Where to start and when to stop timing
column6: Agreed start and finish points make the timing clear.

column2: A feather observation is finished. What should happen before the next group starts?
column3: Return the materials and clear the workspace
column5: Mix the records with another group's notes
column6: Resetting the station keeps the next group's work safe and organised.

column2: A balance tips down on the side holding a pine cone. The other side holds a leaf. What can be recorded?
column3: The pine cone is heavier than the leaf
column4: The leaf is heavier than the pine cone
column6: The lower side of a balance holds the heavier load.

column2: A child measures a stick with blocks but leaves gaps. What needs fixing?
column3: Place the blocks end to end without gaps
column5: Count each gap as a block
column6: Gaps add space that is not part of the measuring units.

column2: A class counts birds for five minutes. A bird cannot be identified. What should the record say?
column3: One unidentified bird was seen
column6: An honest record can state what was seen and what remains unknown.

column2: A tablet video shows a spinner falling. How could replaying it help?
column3: Let children check the movement again
column4: Make the spinner fall more slowly in real life
column6: A video preserves visible details for another look.

column2: Three equal scoops fill a small pot with sand. Which note records the amount?
column3: Pot holds 3 scoops of sand
column6: The note includes the measured amount and the informal unit.

column2: A magnifier shows tiny hairs on a leaf. What should the drawing include?
column3: The hairs in the places they were seen
column6: A scientific drawing records observed details.

column2: A child cannot see the Moon because of clouds. What is an accurate note?
column3: Cloudy: Moon not visible from here
column4: The Moon has disappeared from space
column6: The note records the viewing conditions without inventing a Moon shape.

column2: A pebble sinks and a cork floats in a tub. What should be recorded for each object?
column3: Its name and whether it floated or sank
column5: The same result for both objects
column6: Matching an object with its observation keeps the record useful.

column2: A picture graph uses one leaf picture for one leaf. There are four pictures beside oak. How many oak leaves were counted?
column6: The key says that each picture represents one leaf.

column2: A table lists sponge: bends; stone: does not bend; cloth: bends. Which two belong together by this rule?
column3: Sponge and cloth
column6: Sponge and cloth share the recorded bending property.

column2: Seedling photos are labelled Day 6, Day 1 and Day 3. How should they be placed to show growth over time?
column3: Day 1, Day 3, Day 6
column6: Putting the dates in order shows the observed sequence.

column2: A clear lid bends easily. One group is 'see-through' and another is 'bendy'. Where can the lid go?
column3: In both groups
column5: Only in a group called stone
column6: An object can have more than one recorded property.

column2: A chart records Monday: wet; Tuesday: dry; Wednesday: dry. Which summary matches?
column3: Two dry days and one wet day
column5: One dry day and two wet days
column6: Counting the labels gives two dry observations and one wet observation.

column2: Three tested objects sank and two floated. How many results should appear on the chart?
column6: Both groups together contain five observations.

column2: A class sorts sounds by how they are made. Where does clapping belong?
column3: Hitting surfaces together
column6: Clapping makes sound when the hands strike each other.

column2: A weather chart uses a circle for a sunny day. What should its key explain?
column3: What the circle stands for
column6: A key tells readers what a symbol means.

column2: A child predicted a foil boat would hold four blocks. It held six before sinking. Did the prediction match?
column3: No, it held two more than predicted
column6: Six is two more than four, so the recorded amount differed from the prediction.

column2: One group observes ants for one minute and another for ten minutes. Why might their counts differ?
column3: They watched for different lengths of time
column6: More observation time can allow more visits to be counted.

column2: Two groups test the same magnet. One uses steel clips; the other uses plastic clips. What should they compare first?
column3: The clip materials
column6: Different materials can explain different attraction results.

column2: A class predicts a sponge will return to its shape after a squeeze. It springs back. What does this result show?
column3: The observation matches the prediction
column4: The sponge became a new material
column5: The prediction was made too late
column6: Springing back is the change the class predicted.

column2: A seed investigation has no record for Friday. Can a class claim the seed grew that day?
column3: No, Friday's growth was not recorded
column4: Yes, it can copy Thursday's result
column5: Yes, it can choose any height
column6: Missing observations do not provide evidence for a claim about that day.

column2: A child expected a smooth stone to float. It sank. What further question could be tested?
column3: Do other smooth stones float or sink?
column6: Testing other stones can explore whether smoothness predicts floating.

column2: Children disagree about whether a rattle was louder with more seeds. What could help them check?
column3: Repeat from the same listening place with the same shaking action
column4: Ask who likes the rattle most
column5: Move farther away for only one trial
column6: Keeping the action and listening place similar makes the comparison clearer.

column2: A group compared cloth drying times, but rain wet one sample again. What should their report mention?
column3: Rain changed the conditions for one sample
column5: The slower result should be hidden
column6: The extra rainwater could affect drying time and needs to be reported.

column2: A photo shows a folded card bridge holding three blocks. Which caption fits?
column3: Folded card bridge holding 3 blocks
column6: The caption names what the photograph actually shows.

column2: A class writes instructions for a seed observation. Which opening step is clear?
column3: Place one seed on the damp paper in the labelled dish
column6: The clear step tells the reader what to put where.

column2: A video shows a leaf floating and a pebble sinking. Which spoken sentence fits?
column3: The leaf stayed on top; the pebble went to the bottom
column6: The words describe the two visible outcomes.

column2: A science poster says 'It bent.' The picture shows two strips. What should the writer add?
column3: The name of the strip that bent
column6: Naming the strip removes uncertainty about the result.

column2: A child reports, 'We heard four bird calls in one minute.' What useful detail does 'in one minute' add?
column3: How long the child listened
column4: How far away every bird was
column6: The time tells readers the length of the observation.

column2: A partner cannot read the small labels on a rock drawing. What would help?
column3: Write the labels larger and clearly
column6: Readable labels help someone else understand the drawing.

column2: A class predicts five seeds will sprout, but only three do. Which report tells both facts?
column3: We predicted 5 sprouts and counted 3
column5: We will not report the sprouts
column6: Reporting both numbers makes the prediction and result clear.

column2: A report uses the word 'flexible'. What could help a younger reader understand it?
column3: Add 'able to bend easily'
column4: Replace it with a longer word
column5: Leave out the material being described
column6: A short everyday meaning makes the science word easier to understand.

column2: A sky chart marks a planet beside one star this week and farther from it later. What changed?
column3: The planet's position compared with the stars
column5: The chart proves the stars vanished
column6: Planets can change position against the background stars over time.

column2: A time-lapse shows stars in different places above the same roof during one night. What pattern is being observed?
column3: Stars appear to move across the sky
column4: The roof travels through space alone
column6: Repeated views from one place can show apparent star movement.

column2: The Moon is visible in a blue afternoon sky. Is the observation possible?
column3: Yes, the Moon can sometimes be seen in daylight
column4: No, the Moon only exists at night
column5: No, every daytime object is the Sun
column6: The Moon can be above the horizon and visible during part of the day.

column2: A horizon line is drawn on a sky record. What does it show?
column3: Where the sky appears to meet the land
column6: A horizon gives a reference for describing an object's sky position.

column2: Two Moon photos were taken an hour apart from the same window. The Moon is higher in the second. What can be said?
column3: Its apparent position changed during the hour
column6: The photos show a change in where the Moon appears in the sky.

column2: A class watches a safe sky animation. A labelled point called Venus shifts among the stars over many nights. What is Venus?
column3: A planet
column6: Venus is a planet whose position can be tracked against stars.

column2: A rooftop is included in each night-sky drawing. Why is this useful?
column3: It helps compare where sky objects appear
column6: A fixed landmark helps compare positions between observations.

column2: A planet is hidden behind a tree from one viewing spot. What is a sensible explanation?
column3: The tree blocks the view from that spot
column4: The planet has left the solar system
column5: The tree has swallowed the planet
column6: An object can be present even when something blocks our view.

column2: A teacher plays a speaker beside a paper sheet without touching it. The sheet trembles. What can this show?
column3: Sound energy can make another object vibrate
column4: The paper has become a speaker
column5: Sound can only stay inside the speaker
column6: Sound can travel from a source and cause another object to vibrate.

column2: In a cup-and-string telephone, speech can be heard at the other cup. What carries vibrations between the cups?
column3: The stretched string
column5: The printed letters on the cups
column6: A stretched string can carry vibrations from one cup to the other.

column2: A class hears a recording made by an underwater microphone. What does it show?
column3: Sound can travel through water
column4: Sound exists only in dry air
column6: Underwater sound recordings show that water can carry sound.

column2: A child taps two xylophone bars and hears different notes. What should they compare?
column3: How high or low each note sounds
column5: The length of the tune's name
column6: Different bars can produce notes with different pitches.

column2: A comb makes a buzzing sound when its teeth are gently flicked. Which part vibrates?
column3: The comb's teeth
column4: Only the label on the desk
column6: Flicking makes the teeth move back and forth and produce sound.

column2: A singer makes a low note and then a high note at a similar loudness. What changed?
column3: The pitch
column6: High and low notes have different pitches even at similar loudness.

column2: A teacher rubs two rough wooden blocks together. What action makes the scraping sound?
column3: Rubbing surfaces together
column6: Rubbing rough surfaces can start vibrations that make a scraping sound.

column2: A paper strip buzzes when air is blown past it. What should children look for?
column3: The strip moving back and forth
column6: The moving strip provides evidence of vibration making sound.

column2: A strip of wool is pulled gently but does not get noticeably longer. What was observed?
column3: It did not stretch much in this test
column6: Some materials stretch little under a gentle pull.

column2: A clay tile has a hole pressed through it. What changed?
column3: Its shape, with an opening added
column6: Making an opening changes the shape while the clay remains clay.

column2: A cardboard box is opened along its folds and laid flat. What stayed the same?
column3: It is still cardboard
column4: It still has the same box shape
column5: It is now made of cloth
column6: Unfolding changes the form but not the material.

column2: A paper strip is twisted, while another is bent into an arch. What is different?
column3: The actions used to change their shapes
column4: The paper has become two new materials
column5: Only one strip is still paper
column6: Twisting and bending change shape in different ways.

column2: A soft ball of dough is divided equally into four pieces. What can be observed?
column3: Four smaller pieces of the same dough
column6: Dividing changes the number and size of pieces, not what they are made from.

column2: A craft maker twists plant fibres into cord. What is the purpose of the twisting?
column3: To join and shape fibres into a useful cord
column6: Twisting can change the arrangement of fibres for a useful purpose.

column2: A paper strip tears when pulled, but a fabric strip stays whole. What does this show?
column3: Materials can respond differently to a pull
column4: Every pull changes the material type
column6: The same kind of action can have different effects on materials.

column2: A sculptor adds dents to clay using a blunt tool. What evidence shows the physical change?
column3: The surface has new hollows
column5: The clay is now a star
column6: Dents change the surface shape while the material remains clay.

column2: A family records both school-route travel times on several days. Why use several days?
column3: To see whether a pattern repeats
column4: To make both routes the same length
column6: Several days of records help show whether a travel-time pattern repeats.

column2: One plant has broad leaves and another has narrow leaves. What could the class compare?
column3: The widths of the leaves
column5: Which plant has the nicest name
column6: Leaf width is an observable feature that can be compared.

column2: Birds visit a tree at breakfast and lunch. Which question could a class test by counting?
column3: Are there more bird visits at breakfast or lunch?
column6: Bird visits can be counted for equal observation times and compared.

column2: A class gives similar seedlings different amounts of water. Which prediction fits this question?
column3: Seedlings given some water may grow more than those given none
column4: Every seedling will grow fastest with unlimited water
column5: Watering will turn seedlings into soil
column6: The prediction gives a possible growth difference that can be checked.

column2: A student calls a statement a prediction after seeing the test result. What is the problem?
column3: A prediction should say what may happen before testing
column4: Results should be changed to match predictions
column6: A prediction is made before the outcome is known.

column2: A plant leans towards a window. The pot is turned around. What might new growth do?
column3: Bend towards the light again
column6: The first observation supports a prediction about new growth towards light.

column2: A sharp edge could cut a hand. What is the risk of using it?
column3: Someone could be cut
column4: It must make a loud sound
column6: A risk concerns possible harm; a sharp edge can cause a cut.

column2: One group measures water in large cupfuls and another uses small cupfuls. Why are their counts hard to compare?
column3: Their cupfuls hold different amounts
column6: Informal measures must use the same-sized unit for direct comparison.

column2: A child writes 'a few seeds' after counting exactly eight. Which record is clearer?
column3: 8 seeds
column6: The exact count reports how many seeds were observed.

column2: A child changes a tally just to match another group. Why is that wrong?
column3: The tally no longer shows what the child observed
column4: Every group must get the same count
column6: A tally should record actual observations, even when groups differ.

column2: A class predicts dark cloth will warm faster. Both cloths start at the same temperature and have equal readings at each check. What do the readings show?
column3: This test did not support the prediction
column4: The dark cloth definitely warmed faster
column6: Equal readings at the same times do not show faster warming of the dark cloth.

column2: A class predicts a long-bladed paper spinner will fall more slowly. It takes 4 seconds; the short-bladed one takes 2 seconds from the same height. What happened?
column3: The long-bladed spinner took longer in this test
column4: Both spinners took the same time
column6: Four seconds is longer than two seconds, supporting the prediction in this test.

column2: Cloth absorbed 8 drops and foil absorbed none. Which conclusion matches the result?
column3: The cloth absorbed more drops in this test
column6: The conclusion compares the recorded amounts.

column2: A group's third trial differs from the first two. Which sentence clearly reports this?
column3: Trial 3 was different, so we will check our method
column5: We deleted Trial 3 because it was different
column6: The sentence reports the difference honestly and states a useful next step.

column2: Children predicted 10 bird visits but counted 7. Which sentence tells the difference clearly?
column3: We counted 3 fewer visits than we predicted
column5: We will leave out the count
column6: Seven is three fewer than ten, so the sentence compares the prediction and result.

column2: A class shares a table, a labelled drawing and a short conclusion. How do these help the reader?
column3: They show the evidence and explain the finding
column4: They guarantee the prediction was right
column5: They make all future tests unnecessary
column6: Different forms can work together to communicate the observations and finding.

column2: Which rocky object naturally travels around Earth?
column3: The Moon
column6: The Moon is Earth's natural satellite: it travels around Earth.

column2: A child watches the Moon as thin clouds pass. Its outline is hidden briefly, then visible again. What happened?
column3: Clouds moved across the view of the Moon
column6: A cloud can block the view without changing the Moon itself.

column2: Which safe record could show a daily sky pattern?
column3: Shadow drawings labelled with the observation times
column6: Timed shadow observations can show changes linked to the Sun's apparent position.

column2: A child says the stars are gone during the day. Which explanation is better?
column3: Most are hidden by the bright daytime sky
column4: They disappear from space each morning
column6: Most stars are too faint to see against the bright daytime sky.

column2: Rice grains rest on a drum skin. They jump when the drum is tapped. What moves them?
column3: The vibrating drum skin
column6: The vibrating skin pushes the grains, making the movement visible.

column2: A drum is tapped gently and then more strongly at a safe volume. The second sound is louder. What does this suggest?
column3: A stronger tap can make a larger vibration and a louder sound
column5: The drum has become a new material
column6: A stronger tap can make the drum skin move more and produce a louder sound.

column2: A cardboard tube is squashed flat. What changed?
column3: The tube is flatter than before
column6: Squashing changes the shape of the tube while it remains cardboard.

column2: How can children compare how easily two materials bend?
column3: Use equal-sized strips and the same gentle bending action
column4: Choose the brightest strip without testing
column5: Use different sizes and pushes without recording
column6: Keeping size and action similar makes the bending comparison clearer.

column2: A sky guide labels Jupiter as a planet. What group does Earth also belong to?
column3: Planets in the solar system
column6: Earth and Jupiter are planets in our solar system.

column2: A class records a shadow at breakfast, lunch and afternoon tea. Which record keeps the observations in order?
column3: Breakfast, lunch, afternoon tea
column6: Ordering observations by time helps show the daily change.

column2: A Moon photo is taken beside a hilltop. Another photo shows it farther above the same hill. What does the hill help compare?
column3: The Moon's apparent height in the sky
column5: The Moon's exact distance from Earth
column6: A fixed landmark helps describe changes in apparent sky position.

column2: A cloudy morning leaves no clear pole shadow. What should the class record?
column3: No clear shadow could be measured
column6: Clouds can make shadows faint, so the observation should state the limitation.

column2: A star chart shows the same star group above different landmarks through the night. Which feature stayed recognisable?
column3: The pattern of stars in the group
column4: The group's place above the land
column6: A star group's pattern can remain recognisable while its position appears to change.

column2: Earth, the Moon and the Sun are drawn as equal circles. What must the teacher explain?
column3: Their real sizes are not equal
column5: They are all made of paper
column6: A drawing can label objects without showing their true relative sizes.

column2: A child sees one bright point above a tree. Can brightness alone tell whether it is a planet or a star?
column3: No, more information is needed
column4: Yes, every bright point is a planet
column5: Yes, every bright point is a star
column6: Both planets and stars can look like bright points in the sky.

column2: An evening sky record says 'Moon not seen'. What can the record tell us?
column3: The observer did not see the Moon then
column5: The Moon cannot appear on another evening
column6: Not seeing an object is different from proving it is no longer there.

column2: A metal lid rings when tapped but sounds dull when resting on a thick pad. What does the pad do?
column3: It reduces the lid's vibration
column4: It changes the lid into cloth
column5: It creates a higher note every time
column6: A soft pad can reduce movement and shorten the ringing sound.

column2: A tambourine is shaken and its small metal discs move. What helps make the jingling sound?
column3: The discs hit each other and vibrate
column6: Colliding metal discs vibrate and produce the jingle.

column2: A teacher gently taps a desk while a child listens through the desk surface. What can carry the sound?
column3: The solid desk
column6: Solids can carry vibrations from one place to another.

column2: A sealed shaker contains dry beans. It is tilted slowly, then shaken gently. Why can the sounds differ?
column3: The beans hit the container differently
column6: Changing the action changes the collisions and the sound.

column2: A rubber band is held tightly so it cannot move after plucking. What is likely?
column3: Its sound becomes shorter
column5: It produces a new tune by itself
column6: Stopping the movement reduces the sound-producing vibration.

column2: A child scrunches a sheet of paper, then leaves it still. When is rustling most likely?
column3: While the paper is being scrunched
column4: Only after it has been still for an hour
column6: Scrunching makes parts move and vibrate, producing rustling sounds.

column2: Two recordings play the same note, one softly and one loudly. What difference should be recorded?
column3: Loudness
column5: A change from high to low pitch
column6: The same note can be played at different volumes.

column2: A flute and a drum are played at a comfortable volume. Which action matches the flute?
column3: Blowing air
column6: Blowing starts vibrations in the flute's air to make sound.

column2: A sheet of foil is pressed around a toy to copy its outline. What makes foil useful here?
column3: It can be reshaped
column4: It turns into the toy's material
column6: Foil can keep a changed shape while remaining foil.

column2: A dough ring is pulled until it becomes a longer oval. What happened to its shape?
column3: It became longer in the pulling direction
column5: It did not change at all
column6: Pulling can stretch and reshape soft dough.

column2: A child cuts a circle from card. What are the circle and leftover sheet made from?
column3: The same card
column6: Cutting changes the pieces' shapes but they remain card.

column2: A thin strip is bent into a hook to hang a decoration. Why bend the strip?
column3: To make a shape suited to the job
column5: To make it a new substance
column6: Changing shape can make a material useful for a particular purpose.

column2: A dry twig snaps while a soft stem bends under a gentle push. What differs?
column3: How the materials respond to the push
column4: Whether either object has a shape
column5: Whether the child can see them
column6: Some materials break while others bend under a similar action.

column2: A flat clay piece is curled into a bowl with raised sides. Which change helps it hold beads?
column3: Its new bowl shape
column6: Reshaping clay into a bowl creates sides that can hold objects.

column2: A sponge is compressed under a small block. It becomes tall again when the block is removed. What does this show?
column3: The shape change can be mostly undone
column4: The sponge became a new substance
column6: Some materials spring back when a pushing force is removed.

column2: A long paper chain is cut between two links. What changed?
column3: There are now two shorter chains
column6: Cutting changes the arrangement and length, while the links remain paper.

column2: A triangle is held by its loop, then gripped by its metal side. It rings less when gripped. Why?
column3: The hand reduces the metal's vibration
column4: The loop makes its own music
column5: The metal becomes a new material
column6: Holding the vibrating metal reduces its movement and shortens the ringing sound.
